title: Grants are walked in list order and the last applicable one wins, so MOVE_GRANT can change a verdict without changing any grant
content:
The decision algorithm is a fold over the grant list:

```
decision = deny
for grant in grants (in order):
  if covers(grant, request) and matches(grant.principal, subject, ctx)
     and (grant.where is absent or eval(grant.where, ctx)):
        decision = grant.effect          # the last applicable grant wins
return decision
```

So grants are a **stack**, and evaluation is **default deny, last applicable grant wins**. The `document-acl` demo appends `g-deny-bob` after the `{anyone}` allow on `ADD_ENTRY` — Bob is refused; then moves that deny to index 0 with `MOVE_GRANT` — the later `g-anyone-add` wins again and Bob is back. "Order decides, not existence."

`covers` is where the two subtleties live. A capability whose scope is absent or `"*"` reaches every scope. For `execute`, an absent `operation` list means every operation in the scope. And a read is also covered by an *allow* on execute for that scope (see the note on execute conferring read). `matches` is exact for `{anyone}`, case-insensitive for `{address}`, folded at the operation's position for `{group}`, and a condition evaluation for `{match}`.

Because the rule is positional and a grant can be shadowed by a later deny, "administration is reachable" is a question about the whole list, not about a grant being present — which is what the self-lockout guardrail checks.
